summary:
FireCal shows whether fire activity around Houston is normal for the time of year. Search an area to see fires detected in the past 7 days, a monthly calendar from 2000 to 2026, estimated smoke drift and a 5-day weather outlook.

NASA's fire sensors count differently. For the same Houston area and years, VIIRS records 3.7 times as much burning as MODIS. As MODIS retires, that difference makes older records hard to compare with today. FireCal places both sensors' observations on one 1 km grid, learns how they compare during 2012–2026 and uses that relationship to estimate 2000–2011 on the newer sensor's scale. Estimates include a likely range.

We tested it by setting aside one year at a time, building the conversion from the other years and checking it against the year we set aside. Across 15 test years, yearly totals were typically off by 9%, compared with 72% for unadjusted MODIS. Simply joining the records makes 80% of months since 2012 read "well above normal." With FireCal, 7% do.
details:
What FireCal shows

Search a town, address or coordinates in Greater Houston. You can also use your location, pick a preset or click the map and choose a radius.

Recent fires: See every detection from the past 7 days. Larger flames mean stronger detections. Click one for its time, satellite, fire intensity, wind and humidity.

Smoke drift: Fires detected in the past 2 days show where smoke could travel over the next 3 hours. Each path follows the hourly wind forecast at that fire. Stronger fires and gustier wind produce wider paths.

Normal or unusual: Compare the latest full month with the middle value for the same month in earlier years. FireCal gives a plain answer and shows how much higher or lower it is. It also compares this month so far with the same point in earlier years. Map squares highlight areas with more burning than usual since the start of last month.

Weather: Check current wind and humidity, plus a 5-day outlook for conditions that could help fire spread. The rule is stated on the site.

History: Play the map month by month or drag the timeline to any month. Switch between a plain map, satellite imagery and NASA night lights. The calendar has one colored square per month from 2000 to 2026, plus yearly totals. A circular fire clock shows the same record in a different layout.

Downloads: Save the original NASA detections as CSV, the calendar as CSV or SVG, and the sources and method as JSON. Calendar files label each value as observed, estimated or missing and include likely ranges.

The page opens with a 25-year burning wall for Greater Houston. One square represents one month, with yearly totals above. Switch between the raw records and FireCal to see how the sensor change affects the record. The page also shows the accuracy checks and six use cases with current results for real Houston areas.

The NASA data

We used 137,565 NASA FIRMS detections from November 2000 through November 14, 2026. Of those, 60,642 pass the rules for inclusion. The region extends from 96.2°W to 94.6°W and 29.0°N to 30.9°N.

The records come from MODIS Collection 6.1 on Terra and Aqua, and VIIRS 375 m Collection 2 on Suomi NPP and NOAA-20. Low-confidence detections and fixed heat sources such as refinery flares are excluded from the activity measure. They remain in the downloads.

How we make the records comparable

Every detection goes on the same 1 km grid. A square counts once per satellite per day. The unit is a square kilometer-day of detected fire. We do not add the sensors' counts together.

A month counts as observed only when the satellite was operating and every day's data was retrieved. Missing data stays missing instead of becoming zero.

The years 2012–2026 show how both sensors measured the same area. A statistical model learns the seasonal relationship. A second model combines many small decision trees to improve that estimate. It uses MODIS activity, nearby areas, the months before and after, fire intensity, season and location. If a historical month has more activity than any training example, we keep using the conversion factor learned for the largest training values. This lets the estimate keep increasing.

We use that conversion to estimate 2000–2011 on the VIIRS scale, with a likely range for each estimate.

How we tested it

We set aside one year, built the conversion using the other years and checked the result against VIIRS measurements from the year we set aside. We repeated this for 15 years, from 2012 to 2026. We chose the error measure before looking at the results.

Monthly results: FireCal's error score was 0.218. The seasonal model scored 0.270, one correction factor scored 0.352 and unadjusted MODIS scored 1.403. Lower is better. Converted to a relative scale, those scores correspond to roughly 24% monthly error for FireCal, 42% for one correction factor and a difference of 4.1 times for unadjusted MODIS.

Yearly results: Yearly totals were typically off by 9% with FireCal, 10% with one correction factor and 72% with unadjusted MODIS.

Checking the improvement: We repeated the comparison using different groups of whole test years. The 95% range for FireCal's error minus the seasonal model's error was −0.087 to −0.023. The whole range is below zero, which supports the improvement over that model.

Effect on the verdict: We counted months since 2012 with at least twice the middle value for the same month in earlier years. Simply joining MODIS and VIIRS flags 80% of months as well above normal. FireCal flags 7%. This measures how often the flag appears, not a verified false-alarm rate.

Keeping the record going

Suomi NPP stopped on November 2, 2026. NOAA-20 now provides the VIIRS reference. Across 103 months when both were available, NOAA-20 recorded 105% of Suomi NPP's activity. Their month-to-month rankings closely matched, with a rank correlation of 0.94.

Who can use it

Emergency managers can check whether this month's burning is unusual. Forestry and land managers can see the local burn season. Farmers can compare crop-residue burning with earlier years. The same record can help electric utilities, insurers, air-quality teams and public-health staff. This prototype covers Greater Houston. The method can be applied wherever NASA FIRMS has data.

Tools and source code

Python, NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn and Requests handle the data and models. TypeScript, Vite and Leaflet run the website. Esri and OpenStreetMap provide basemaps, Nominatim provides place search and Open-Meteo provides weather forecasts. NASA GIBS supplies the night imagery. GitHub Pages hosts the site. Pillow and SciPy help draw the deck map. The deck is HTML printed to PDF with Chromium.

Source code: https://github.com/blazepatrol/firecal

Limits

FireCal measures burning detected by satellites. It does not count separate fires or measure burned area or the chance of ignition. Clouds and smoke can hide fires. Smoke paths and the fire-spread outlook are simple estimates from forecast wind, humidity and rain. They are not official forecasts or full smoke models. Smoke paths assume the fire is still burning.

Estimates before 2012 assume the relationship learned from later years also held earlier. Fire observations on the site stop at November 14, 2026. Weather forecasts update live.
